study.title: 1 Corinthians 13 The most excellent way: love
study.overview: Paul interrupts the subject of spiritual gifts to show that, without love, the most impressive gifts lose their value. In the first three verses, he states that eloquence, prophecy, knowledge, extraordinary faith, extreme generosity and even martyrdom take advantage of nothing if they are not accompanied by love. Then he describes Christian love not as an abstract feeling, but as a concrete way of acting: patient, kind, humble, without envy, without arrogance, without selfishness, without grudge, without pleasure in injustice. Finally, the apostle contrasts what is partial and temporary with what remains: prophecies, tongues and knowledge will be set aside, but faith, hope and love continue; and the greatest of them is love.

outline.title: Without love, the biggest gifts are worth nothing
outline.explanation: Paul uses strong examples to show that even admired spiritual abilities - languages, prophecy, knowledge, miraculous faith, total best and extreme sacrifice - do not benefit before God or the church when they lack love and correct motivation.

outline.title: The practical love marks
outline.explanation: The text does not define love for theory, but by attitudes. Love is revealed in patience, kindness, humility, purity of intent, self-control, joy with the truth and perseverance that endures and hopes.

outline.title: What remains forever
outline.explanation: Gifts have limited duration and serve the current stage of Christian life. As our knowledge is partial, they will be overcome when it comes what is complete. Love does not fail; therefore, between faith, hope and love, love is the greatest.

study.context: In this chapter, Paul resumes and deepens the discussion of spiritual gifts initiated in the previous chapter. The notes indicate that the Corinthians especially valued languages, prophecy and knowledge, which generated pride and division. The apostle responds by showing that the supreme criterion is not the appearance of spiritual power, but the presence of true love among Christians.
study.theology: The chapter teaches that love is the moral essence of Christian life and the right foundation for the use of any gift. It is not presented as mere emotion, but as a willingness to seek the good of the other, subordinating personal desires to the common good. Theologically, this means that spiritual gifts do not define the value of the believer before God. There is also a distinction between what is partial, appropriate to the present time, and what is full and permanent. Faith, hope and love are virtues that remain, but love is the greatest because it expresses more directly the character of God and the standard of Christian communion.

scholarViews.insight: Paul interrupts the discussion of spiritual gifts to show that love is more important than any gift and that without love, spiritual gifts have no value.
Love is described as a benevolent disposition toward God and with others; it is the most excellent and superior form to all gifts.
Even eloquence, prophecy, knowledge, miraculous faith, extreme generosity and martyrdom do not take advantage for salvation if they lack love for God and others.

questions: What forms of Christian service can seem spiritual, but being done without true love?
What traits of love in 1 Corinthians 13:4-7 else confront their current behavior?
How does the truth that gifts are partial helps the church to value love more than spiritual prestige?
study.practice: Choose a concrete relationship this week - family, church, work or study - and practice a specific expression of love described in the chapter: hearing without seeking advantage, answering without irritation, acting patiently or cheerful with the truth rather than defending the ego itself. When evaluating your ministries, ask not only what you do, but what spirit you do. The chapter calls the Christian to measure maturity less for capacity and more for consistent love.
study.uncertainty: The given notes do not explain in detail the expression about what is 'complete' in verse 10; therefore, it is appropriate to avoid defining it accurately beyond what the text itself states. There is also no basis in the notes to establish a more specific historical scenario than the general situation of division and undue valuation of gifts in the church of Corinth.
